title: From punk to now: a small scene that kept the doors open to all ages.
body: Salt Lake punk was never big. It lasted because there was always a room for kids too young for bars, and that's still how it works.

notes: You asked how punk turns into today's scene, so this slide replaces the old lane opener with the evolution. The thread is all-ages access: the Indian Center in the 80s, Kilby Court's garage since 1999, DIY halls now. The 90s row is honest on purpose. Straight edge is part of local identity, but the violence and the 1998 killing are why the lane uses the X only as an all-ages hand stamp and never as a crew mark. title: What the scene is now: small, DIY, mostly hardcore, still all-ages.
body: There isn't one Salt Lake punk scene in 2026. There are a few small ones that share rooms, plus a big festival on top.
points: **Hardcore is the most active part, and it's DIY.** Shows at Fellowship Hall, Olifer, Black Lung Society and Pineyard, and Hardcore Halloween at Kilby every October (verify 2026).
**Punk is smaller and overlaps riot grrrl.** P.S. Destroy This is the band City Weekly picked for 2026. Promoters Hypha, Yardwork and Joz Presents book a lot of the small shows.
**Indie is the public face.** Kilby Court turned 25, and Kilby Block Party drew 25,000 to 30,000 a day in 2026 with Turnstile on the bill next to Lorde.
**It's small, and that's the point.** A hall show is maybe a few dozen to a couple hundred people (estimate, verify). SLUG and City Weekly cover it, and touring bands play Soundwell and The Depot.
**What makes it Salt Lake.** All-ages rooms, the straight-edge legacy, making your own spaces, being the weird kid in a religious town, and skating or riding in the morning before a show at night.
notes: The comment asked whether the current scene is hardcore. Mostly, yes, at the DIY level, sitting inside a much bigger indie and festival world. Saying it's small is part of the case: the lane should look like it came out of a hall show, not a mall. We don't use any real band names or logos on product. If we want scene credibility, we pay and credit local flyer artists and promoters, or partner with Kilby or SLUG on a small run. Current venue status and crowd sizes are marked verify until a local confirms them.
